Integration of a deal this size is rarely seamless, and the company acknowledged near-term frictions tied to accounting, synergy capture and the mechanics of merging two large organizations. Even so, the company stressed that the combination was tracking ahead of its own internal markers on cost savings and volume contribution. The Guyana stake in particular gives the firm a growth engine with low supply costs, a feature that stood out sharply in a quarter where the crude benchmark offered little tailwind. Through the Hess combination, the company now carries a sizeable interest in the Stabroek block offshore Guyana, one of the most consequential crude discoveries of the past decade. That geographic spread gives the company a buffer against any single region's swings, and the company underscored how the enlarged portfolio blends mature cash generators with fresh growth barrels. The result is an upstream engine built to throw off cash across a range of price environments rather than betting everything on one basin. Beyond the wellhead, the company operates a substantial refining and marketing arm that turns crude into fuels and offers them through a vast retail network. Those downstream units give the business a counterweight when crude pricing compresses, because fuel margins often move on their own cycle. The quarter saw the refining arm process heavy volumes, adding a steadying layer to the overall result even as the upstream benchmark stayed muted. Natural gas and liquefied gas also feature prominently in the mix, tied to projects that feed power grids and export markets. That financial cushion has long defined how the firm approaches the business, letting it keep funding advantaged projects even when prices dip. The quarter reinforced that discipline, with the company stressing that a strong balance sheet lets the company act from strength rather than scramble whenever the benchmark turns lower. title: ExxonMobil Stock Trades at a Premium: Is It Still Worth Buying? - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM stock is trading at an 8.59x trailing 12-month Enterprise Value to Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EV/EBITDA), which is a premium compared with the broader industry average of 6.66x. BP plcBP and ChevronCVX, belonging to the same space, are trading at 2.69x and 7.36x, respectively. Is it worth buying XOM at a premium price right away? To find out, let’s delve into the business fundamentals and the overall crude pricing environment as the integrated energy giant generates the king size of its earnings from upstream operations. West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude is trading at more than $98 per barrel. The high prices are being driven by intensifying conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. Energy Information Administration in its latest short-term energy outlook projected WTI at $88.21 per barrel this year, higher than $65.40 last year. A highly favorable oil pricing environment is likely to continue supporting ExxonMobil’s exploration and production activities, similar to BP and Chevron. Image Source: The U.S. Energy Information Administration The company has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing new drilling techniques and artificial intelligence to boost and optimize production volumes at lower cost structures. On its third-quarter 2026 call, the integrated major mentioned that in the prolific basin it is now operating three automated drilling rigs, and planning to increase the count to 25% of the total fleet in the basin next year. By 2028, ExxonMobil is planning to boost the proportion to 50%, to further lower its cost structures amid technological advancements. Considering its downstream business, ExxonMobil's investments in upgrading its U.S. refineries should help the company produce more high-value fuels, particularly diesel. By making better use of existing facilities, XOM can expand output without the high costs of building new refineries. These improvements are expected to support stronger profit margins and cash flow over the long term. Moreover, XOM has a strong balance sheet, on which it could rely when the business environment turns unfavorable. During the September quarter of this year, the company lowered its debt by more than $9 billion. Considering the price chart, ExxonMobil has jumped 57.6% over the past year, outpacing the industry’s 57.3% growth. BP and Chevron have gained 36.3% and 48.8%, respectively, over the same period. With the outperformance, XOM stock is currently pricey. But it is worth paying the premium since the outlook for the company’s overall business environment seems bright. title: Did Earnings Beat Just Shift Chevron (CVX) Investment Narrative? - Simply Wall St

To own Chevron here, you need to be comfortable with a business that leans on large, long life oil and gas projects, a disciplined dividend and heavy exposure to refining cycles. The short term swing factor is whether record refining profitability and Venezuela production plans can offset any soft spots in upstream volumes and future demand questions for hydrocarbons. The biggest risk right now is simple. If energy demand shifts faster than Chevron reshapes its project mix, the firm could feel pressure on revenue and margins even with strong current cash generation. Recent Q3 strength and ETF flows update that debate but do not fundamentally change it. The governance announcement around Siva Barnwell Adams becoming corporate secretary and chief governance officer matters more than it might seem at first glance. Chevron is committing billions to Venezuela, expanding exploration across several regions and integrating prior deals, so board level oversight and legal discipline sit directly on the critical execution path. Barnwell Adams brings long experience inside Chevron across major transactions, joint ventures and corporate matters, while Mary Francis will remain as senior advisor into 2027. For you as a shareholder, that combination points to continuity around how large projects are structured, how governance risk is managed and how the board evaluates future catalysts and downside scenarios. Cronk through the analyst model and Chevron suddenly looks less like a pure refinery story and more like a long run earnings puzzle. Consensus expects revenue to edge lower by 1.2% per year over the next three years, even as profit margins are projected to shift from 9.8% today to 12.6% in the same window. On the earnings line, forecasts point to net income of US$25.5b by 2029 compared with US$20.6b today. That is an increase of about US$4.9b in profit, with earnings per share expected to reach US$13.83. Behind those headline numbers sits a wide spread of views, from US$18.7b at the cautious end of the range to US$33.1b at the most optimistic. Chevron's narrative projects US$202.0b revenue and US$25.5b earnings by 2029. This aligns with expectations for revenue to decline by 1.2% per year and implies an earnings increase of about US$4.9b from US$20.6b today. Analysts then link those outcomes to a P/E of 20.8x on the 2029 earnings, compared with 21.7x today and above the 12.6x level quoted for the broader US oil and gas group. That setup assumes investors keep paying a premium multiple for Chevron, even though the top line is modeled to contract modestly while profitability does more of the heavy lifting. The Simply Wall St Community contributes three Chevron fair value views, stretching from US$232.50 up to about US$369.69, so some members see limited upside while others model far richer outcomes. title: Chevron Earnings Call Highlights Cash, Growth and Resilience - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron ((CVX)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call. Chevron’s Earnings Call Signals Strong Momentum Despite Market Risks Chevron’s earnings call carried a strongly positive tone, led by robust cash generation, a stronger balance sheet, steady production and record refining and natural gas output. Management also highlighted AI gains and broad growth opportunities, although lower sequential earnings, volatile commodity prices, permitting issues and a future non-cash accounting loss remain notable risks. Chevron reported third-quarter earnings of $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share, while adjusted earnings reached $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share. Cash flow from operations excluding working capital was $16.6 billion, and adjusted free cash flow totaled $14.2 billion. Chevron reduced debt by more than $3 billion and increased cash by more than $4 billion during the quarter. Net debt to cash flow from operations improved to 0.4 times, giving the company greater financial flexibility. Third-quarter production was nearly 4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day despite entitlement impacts and planned maintenance turnarounds. U.S. upstream output stayed above 2 million barrels per day for the fifth consecutive quarter. Chevron posted record quarterly natural gas production of more than 9 billion cubic feet per day, led by Australia and the Eastern Mediterranean. Its U.S. Gulf of America operations also set a new quarterly deepwater production record. Permian production remained above 1 million barrels per day for a sixth straight quarter. Capital spending per barrel improved by more than 25%, while drilling and completion spending fell 40% and facility spending declined 50%. Chevron expanded its acreage and secured new fiscal terms in Venezuela, making the business more competitive and immediately accretive to free cash flow. The company plans to double production from its three joint ventures to about 600,000 barrels per day by 2031, with total costs below $20 per barrel. Chevron is on track to reach roughly 300,000 barrels per day of gross Venezuelan production by year-end, up 20% in 12 months. It markets all crude from the three ventures, with most volumes shipped to U.S. refineries. A planned 50% reduction in Bakken midstream tariffs should improve returns, expand economic inventory and increase operating flexibility. Chevron plans to reduce its rig count from three to two while sustaining about 180,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. The Hess Midstream restructuring is expected to increase corporate return on capital employed by 0.5% and deconsolidate $3.7 billion of debt. Chevron also expects recurring earnings and an immediate improvement in Bakken upstream earnings and cash flow after the transaction. Chevron achieved record crude throughput across its refining system and record quarterly U.S. crude throughput. More than 80% of U.S. refinery turnarounds over the past two years were completed with first-quartile duration, supporting reliability. A proprietary catalyst at Chevron’s largest U.S. refineries lifted distillate production by 10% after changes to cut points. Third-quarter distillate yield at those refineries reached 46%, while Pascagoula recorded its strongest diesel production in at least three or four years. Chevron accelerated debottlenecking at Pasadena, adding about 15% of refinery capacity at nominal cost. The company also plans to increase Pascagoula capacity by another 7% by 2030. Upstream debottlenecking projects added more than 85,000 barrels per day of capacity. TCO’s third-generation plant gained 20% of capacity, Ballymore rose 7%, and Anchor increased capacity by 33%, or 25,000 barrels per day. Chevron added 22 million acres over the past two years, doubling its exploration footprint across 12 new basins. In the latest quarter, it added six Gulf of America blocks as well as acreage in Angola, Nigeria, Guinea-Bissau and Egypt. The company made 15 infrastructure-led discoveries over two years with a 40% success rate, above the industry average. AI pattern recognition found more than 150 leads in the Gulf of America, with 16 prospects advancing to evaluation and 30 net new prospects identified. Chevron said AI generated more than $100 million of value capture year to date in 2026. In the DJ Basin, the technology cut loss-production events by 50%, while AI-enabled production optimization is now deployed in the Permian, Bakken and PZ assets. Chevron’s ApEx system uses four petabytes of data and a century of company knowledge to assemble basin information in hours rather than months. ScoutAI can build basin assessments in hours instead of weeks and is now deployed in 10 new basins. Advanced Chemicals increased cumulative oil-equivalent production in the Permian by as much as 23% during the first 12 months. Chevron is also testing next-generation chemistry through field pilots to improve recovery further. Predictive maintenance, centralized data and AI-supported decisions helped keep Australian LNG reliability strong. Gorgon and Wheatstone operated above nameplate capacity, and the combined assets delivered record third-quarter production. Chevron reaffirmed its framework of consistent dividend growth, efficient investment, a strong balance sheet and share repurchases through the cycle. The company has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years and plans to keep annual buybacks in the $2.5 billion-to-$3 billion range. Organic capital expenditures totaled $3.9 billion in the quarter. Fourth-quarter spending is expected to rise in line with seasonal trends, but full-year capital expenditures are still expected to finish at the low end of annual guidance. Project Kilby is a 2.67-gigawatt, behind-the-meter power project in West Texas backed by a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft. Chevron is targeting a final investment decision, first power in 2028 and full energization in 2031, with potential expansion to combined-cycle power. Chevron said terms in Iraq currently appear more attractive than they have historically and that it is working with the ministry on a development plan. The company is also discussing similar opportunities with several Middle Eastern governments, building a pipeline of growth options beyond 2030. A significant share of Chevron’s fleet is owned or covered by long-term charters agreed before the conflict, at pre-conflict rates. Controlled transportation and greater use of equity crude, which has reached about 50% at times at certain refineries, are supporting current results. Adjusted third-quarter earnings were $1.6 billion below the prior quarter. The decline shows that strong operating performance did not fully offset a less favorable pricing and timing environment. Adjusted upstream earnings fell because of lower realizations, reduced liftings and unfavorable timing effects. Lower depreciation, depletion and amortization expenses and tax benefits partly offset those pressures. Working capital was negatively affected by sharp commodity price increases late in the quarter. Management said rising prices can create additional timing effects, while those impacts generally unwind when prices fall. When the Hess Midstream transaction closes, Chevron expects a one-time non-cash after-tax loss of $3 billion to $4 billion. Management emphasized that the charge reflects deconsolidation accounting rather than the underlying economics of the deal. Management cited a $64 intra-quarter price spread, with crude prices ranging from $68 to $132 per barrel during the quarter. Chevron said the volatility has not changed its short-term capital allocation approach. Chevron expects refining margins to eventually moderate as refinery runs recover and exports increase. Petrochemical markets could also return to oversupply as trade flows normalize, although margins may remain somewhat elevated through year-end and possibly into next year. Project Kilby requires additional permits beyond those already being pursued. AI-driven basin assessments and real-time drilling optimization have accelerated prospect identification and improved exploration outcomes. Bakken operational and financial improvements: The restructuring of Hess Midstream contracts halved midstream tariffs, strengthening Bakken's competitiveness and operational flexibility. Management expects further gains through optimized development plans, long lateral drilling, and integration with advanced chemical technologies. Chevron's outlook centers on scaling efficient production, leveraging digital tools, and navigating market and geopolitical dynamics to sustain profitability. Technology-driven production gains: Management plans to increase Venezuela and Permian output through factory-style drilling and advanced recovery methods, while AI-powered optimization tools are expected to deliver ongoing cost savings and production efficiencies. These efforts are designed to extend asset life and sustain plateau production in key regions. Disciplined capital allocation: Leadership reiterated a commitment to maintaining low net debt, consistently growing dividends, and investing efficiently in both organic and inorganic opportunities. The company anticipates continued volatility in global markets, underscoring the importance of its balanced capital allocation framework to support long-term growth and shareholder returns. title: Exxon's Refining Profits Soared—Did Chevron Get the Same Windfall? - MarketBeat
content:
The biggest question for investors is not whether Exxon's refining business has been thriving thanks in large part to record crack spreads amid the Iran war, but how much of the earnings from these operations reached the company's bottom line, and how long that benefit is likely to last. Since competitor Chevron NYSE: CVX reported its Q3 2026 earnings results on the same day, it provides a useful point of comparison. Ultimately, Exxon's refining and marketing earnings have surpassed its upstream earnings, but the favorable mix may not continue forever. Exxon posted its largest year-to-date (YTD) refining operational performance ever, contributing to $17.5 billion in adjusted Q3 2026 earnings. Breaking down these earnings by segment shows just how dramatically refining has impacted the company's overall performance. The company's Energy Products segment includes its refining and marketing operations; this portion of Exxon's business reached $9 billion in adjusted earnings for Q3, more than double what it was last year at this time. Meanwhile, the company's upstream business, including its core exploration and production operations, came in at $7.3 billion in adjusted earnings for the quarter, down from $9.2 billion in Q2 2026. This decline was substantially wider than Exxon had indicated in its pre-earnings report. In other words, Exxon's Energy Products segment became the company's largest earnings generator for the company this quarter. While this has been a boon for the company, it leaves it exposed if fuel margins should fade. At the same time, the company still produced about 4.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day—though this is about flat on a sequential basis, it nonetheless indicates that there are not necessarily major issues with Exxon's upstream operations for investors to worry about. For this firm, production remained the largest contributor to overall earnings. Chevron's upstream operations generated about $5.7 billion in reported earnings for Q3, while its downstream operations (including refining) yielded $4.9 billion. The company also saw a heavy downward swing for its upstream earnings compared to Q2 2026, as the figure fell from $8.2 billion at that time. Notably, though, downstream earnings was essentially flat from Q2 to Q3 2026. International downstream earnings actually declined on a sequential basis, offsetting gains made in the domestic portion of Chevron's business, which processed about 1.1 million barrels per day at about 98% utilization. Russian diesel waivers and the potential for normalized Gulf shipping may help to ease the tight fuel supply in the months to come. Margins may still remain elevated, however, if geopolitical stressors continue or if refinery output from Russia remains limited. There is also strong seasonal demand to look ahead to, although a historically heavy El Niño may throw off predictions for energy usage. If margins normalize, investors will probably look more to the pace at which these firms buy shares back and how they spend their capital. Both enter the end of the year with significant capacity to generate cash. Exxon has a $20-billion 2027 buyback plan that seems to suggest management is confident the company will continue to print cash, as well as an investment program that should help to improve refinery efficiency. Chevron bought back $2.5 billion in shares last quarter, slightly lower than the previous period, but it is pushing more money toward upstream development. Investors should keep an eye on buyback plans and how they compare to distributions that are tied to temporary commodity market conditions. Additionally, diesel inventories and Russian export volumes will help to assess the impact of global conditions on both companies' margins. Alongside others in the oil and gas space, there are plenty of reasons for investors to be pleased with recent performance, although the big question is whether these companies can maintain their momentum. title: 5 revealing analyst questions from Chevron’s Q3 earnings call - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron’s third quarter results drew a positive response from the market, reflecting outperformance versus Wall Street’s expectations. Management highlighted that operational discipline and strong execution across both upstream and downstream segments were critical in achieving these results. CEO Mike Wirth pointed to Chevron’s record crude throughput in refining and sustained U.S. upstream production, while Vice Chairman Mark Nelson emphasized the impact of AI-driven reliability improvements and debottlenecking projects. The company’s expanded activity in Venezuela and the commissioning of new facilities also contributed to quarterly momentum. Is now the time to buy CVX? Find out in our full research report (it’s free for active Edge members). While we enjoy listening to the management’s commentary, our favorite part of earnings calls is the analyst questions. Those are unscripted and can often highlight topics that management teams would rather avoid or topics where the answer is complicated. Here is what has caught our attention. Arun Jayaram (JPMorgan) asked about Venezuela’s cost structure and risk management; CEO Mike Wirth explained risk is mitigated through strong contract terms and local engagement, while CFO Eimear Bonner confirmed costs are below $20 per barrel, with investments recovering quickly. Devin McDermott (Morgan Stanley) inquired about the TCO concession extension in Kazakhstan; Wirth said discussions are progressing, with narrowed issues and both sides seeking a competitive, mutually beneficial agreement.
